![](sweetspot.svg){width=100% fig-alt="Cartoon of a column of CO₂ molecules between the surface and the top of the atmosphere, each sending one photon straight up. Both photons from the optically thin top layer escape to space, five of the eight from the τ ≈ 1 layer escape, and none of the 27 from the optically thick layers below escape."}

Each CO₂ molecule emits one photon straight up, and the photon is absorbed by
the first molecule directly above it. Optical depth τ is measured downward from
the top of the atmosphere (TOA), so it is small near the top and large near the
surface.

- **Optically thin (τ ≪ 1):** both photons emitted here escape to space, but
  there are only two molecules to emit them.
- **τ ≈ 1:** eight molecules emit, and five of their photons escape.
- **Optically thick (τ ≫ 1):** 27 molecules emit, and every one of their
  photons is absorbed before it gets out.

Five of the seven photons that reach space therefore come from the τ ≈ 1 layer.
Higher up there are too few emitters, and lower down there is too much absorber
overhead. In a real atmosphere, emission to space per unit height likewise
peaks near τ ≈ 1.

Each photon's color shows which layer emitted it: blue for the optically thin
layer, purple for the τ ≈ 1 layer and red for the optically thick layers. The
colors go from coldest to warmest, since temperature falls with height in the
troposphere.

The [notes for instructors](instructor-notes.qmd) cover what the cartoon
simplifies, the physics behind it and some discussion questions, and give a
caption and alt text ready to paste.

## Credit

The figure redraws Fig. 3 of Nadir Jeevanjee, "Climate sensitivity from
radiative-convective equilibrium: A chalkboard approach," *American Journal of
Physics* **91**, 731–745 (2023), <https://doi.org/10.1119/5.0135727>, the
article's cartoon of emission to space from layers of increasing optical depth.
The article is © 2023 its author and published under the
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) license. My changes:
the original's three panels became a single column, the τ ≈ 1 layer now sends
more photons to space than the optically thin layer (in the original each sends
three), the molecules are drawn as linear O=C=O, and each photon's color shows
the layer that emitted it.

My own work on the figure is in the public domain under CC0, like the rest of
this gallery. If you reuse the figure, please keep the credit to Jeevanjee's
article.

## Changing it

The layout, the positions of the optically thin and τ ≈ 1 molecules, and the
height and molecule count of each optically thick row are constants near the
top of `make_sweetspot.py`, which needs only Python and NumPy. The optically
thick molecules are scattered at random about their rows. An optional argument
sets the random seed, which defaults to 5, and some seeds find no valid
placement. The script stops with an error, before it writes `sweetspot.tex`,
if a photon would escape or be absorbed other than as intended or if two
molecules would overlap. Compile `sweetspot.tex` with any LaTeX engine, for
example `pdflatex sweetspot.tex`. The
[design notes](https://github.com/spencerahill/gallery/blob/main/figures/tau1-sweetspot-schematic/design-notes.md)
give the reasons behind each choice in the drawing.
